You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Diagnosis:

The failing test checks that the optimization using the SimplexSolver returns a correct solution with the final variable at 1.0. The test setup uses a LinearObjectiveFunction with some constraints and expects a minimized solution satisfying them.

The SimplexSolver.optimize method calls doOptimize(), which creates a SimplexTableau instance representing the problem. The solver proceeds with solvePhase1 to find a feasible starting solution if there are artificial variables. It performs iterations until the solution is optimal.

The getSolution method in SimplexTableau extracts the solution once optimality is reached. It retrieves the solution values for the original decision variables by locating their basic rows in the tableau and reading the values from the right-hand side column (RHS offset). It accounts for whether variables are restricted to non-negative or not.

The doIteration method performs a single simplex iteration step by selecting pivot column and row, performing row operations to set the pivot element to 1, and zeroing the rest in that column.

The getBasicRow method tries to identify if a column is basic by checking if exactly one row has a non-zero entry in that column. If more than one row has non-zero entries, it returns null meaning no unique basic row.

The observed failure could arise if the algorithm incorrectly identifies basic rows or does not pivot correctly, leading to an incorrect tableau and thus wrong solution values read out. Specifically, getBasicRow returns null if multiple non-zero entries are found in a column, which leads to coefficients[i] being set zero in getSolution. This can cause some variables to be assigned zero when they should have actual values, producing an inaccurate solution.

Hence, the root cause is likely a faulty simplex iteration or tableau update that yields non-basic columns incorrectly represented as basic or the algorithm failing to find the pivot row/column properly, eventually producing the wrong solution vector.

No recent bug reports seem directly related to simplex optimization errors, so those can be considered unrelated here. The current problem is centered on the internals of SimplexSolver, SimplexTableau, and simplex iteration logic.

The main methods related to the processing of the solution and iteration are SimplexSolver.doOptimize(), SimplexSolver.solvePhase1(), SimplexSolver.doIteration(), SimplexTableau.getSolution(), SimplexTableau.getBasicRow(). The analysis points to possible mishandling in these areas causing the solver to return incorrect solutions.

Therefore, the bug likely occurred due to improper simplex tableau updates or incorrect identification of basic variables during pivoting or solution extraction, causing the solver to produce a wrong minimal solution. This results in the test failure asserting solution.getPoint()[2] == 1.0 not holding true.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
